About This Part
Volume 7A establishes the operating model required before an engineer deploys production workloads in
Microsoft Azure. It begins with cloud and Azure fundamentals, then moves through global infrastructure,
tenant and subscription hierarchy, administrative tools, identity, authorization, governance, compute,
networking, and financial controls. The central theme is controlled administration. A secure Azure environment separates human identities from
workload identities, uses explicit scopes for access and policy, standardizes resource organization, designs for
failure domains, and gives every resource an owner, purpose, lifecycle, and cost signal. Scope and Safety

Use a sandbox subscription, Azure free account, Azure for Students subscription, or an organization-
approved training environment. Current eligibility, credits, regional service availability, quotas, and pricing
must be verified before creating resources.

Enable multifactor authentication, protect privileged roles, and use Microsoft Entra groups, Azure RBAC,
managed identities, and just-in-time elevation instead of shared accounts or embedded secrets.

Choose a permitted Azure region and verify availability-zone and service support. Region availability and
service capabilities change over time.

Apply budgets, expiry tags, and cleanup procedures before creating chargeable resources. Stopped virtual
machines can continue to incur storage and networking charges unless they are deallocated and unused
resources are removed.

Do not expose SSH or RDP broadly to the internet. Prefer Azure Bastion, private connectivity, Just-in-Time
access, or tightly restricted source addresses in approved environments.

Chapter 1 - Cloud Computing and Microsoft Azure
Understanding the operating model before choosing services
Learning Objectives

Explain cloud computing through shared responsibility, elasticity, measured consumption, and automation.

Compare IaaS, PaaS, SaaS, serverless, public cloud, private cloud, hybrid cloud, and multicloud.


1.1 Why Cloud Engineering Is an Operating Model
Cloud is not simply rented hardware. It changes how teams request capacity, govern access, deploy changes,
observe health, recover from failure, and allocate cost. In a traditional data center, provisioning often depends
on procurement and manual configuration. In Azure, an authenticated API request can create networks,
compute, databases, identities, and policies in minutes. The speed creates business value only when security,
standards, automation, and ownership are designed at the same time. Why before how Learning a portal workflow without understanding lifecycle, identity, failure boundaries,
and cost creates fragile environments. Professional cloud engineering starts with desired outcomes,
constraints, and evidence.

1. What is the main difference between IaaS and PaaS?
IaaS gives the customer more control and more operating responsibility, including guest OS and middleware. PaaS removes much of that platform administration so teams focus on application code, data, and service
configuration.
2. Why can cloud speed increase risk?
APIs allow resources and privileges to be created quickly. Without policy, least privilege, logging, budgets,
and automated standards, mistakes scale as rapidly as valid delivery.
3. When is rehosting appropriate?
When time, compatibility, or data-center exit urgency dominates and the workload can operate acceptably
without immediate redesign. It should still have a later optimization plan.
4. What does shared responsibility mean?
Microsoft secures and operates the cloud platform according to the service model, while the customer
remains responsible for areas such as identities, data, configuration, application security, and guest OS
management where applicable.

2.1 Azure Geographies, Regions, and Zones
An Azure geography is a market and data-residency boundary that contains one or more regions. A region is a
geographic area containing datacenters connected through a high-capacity network. Many regions provide
availability zones: separate groups of datacenters with independent power, cooling, and network infrastructure. Zones reduce the probability that one localized failure removes every instance of a workload. Critical distinction A region or zone is not a backup strategy. Availability protects service continuity;
backup protects recoverability of data and configuration. Production systems normally need both.

2.2 Zonal and Zone-Redundant Resources
A zonal resource is pinned to a selected zone; the customer deploys enough instances across zones and manages
distribution. A zone-redundant service replicates or distributes across zones as part of the managed service. The
exact capability differs by service, SKU, and region, so support must be verified rather than assumed.

1. What is an Azure availability zone?
A separated group of datacenters within a region with independent power, cooling, and network
infrastructure, used to isolate localized failures.
2. Does deploying to three zones automatically make an application highly available?
No. The application, load distribution, state, data, dependencies, identity, and operations must all survive and
recover from failure.
3. What is the difference between RTO and RPO?
RTO measures acceptable restoration time; RPO measures acceptable data loss expressed as time since the
last recoverable point.

Azure capabilities, SKUs, availability-zone support, quotas, and previews vary by region and can change over

3.3 Resource Group Lifecycle Principle
A resource group should usually contain resources that share a lifecycle and administrative context. Deleting a
resource group initiates deletion of contained resources, subject to locks and service-specific dependencies. Placing a long-lived shared network and a short-lived application in the same resource group can create risky
cleanup and ownership conflicts.
